items.title: Pro-Active Approach in the Context of Quality 5.0 Challenges
items.abstract: This study examines entrepreneurs’ awareness and preventive activities regarding the environment and employees as key elements of the Quality 5.0 concept. Quantitative research was conducted among 380 manufacturing companies in Greater Poland that had not implemented or certified a quality management system. Data were collected using CATI interviews using an original questionnaire assessing the importance and implementation of 24 preventive management factors, with a detailed analysis of 10 factors. The findings identify maintaining good relations with the environment (K2), careful supplier selection and continuous evaluation (K3), improving employee qualifications and skills (K7), and ensuring occupational safety and ergonomics (K8) as the most important preventive management factors. The combined IPA and paired analyses identify K7—improving employee qualifications and skills—as the clearest improvement priority: it was the only factor in the “concentrate here” quadrant, had the largest importance–implementation gap (0.34), and the largest rank-biserial effect (rrb = 0.639). K2—maintaining good relations with the environment—and K8—ensuring occupational safety and ergonomics—combined high importance with high implementation and should therefore be maintained, while K5—selection of employees based on their competencies—also warrants attention due to its gap of 0.28. Paired Wilcoxon tests showed statistically significant implementation shortfalls for all ten factors after Holm correction, indicating that the gap between perceived importance and implementation is systematic. Participatory management (K6) received the lowest importance and implementation ratings, although its large paired effect suggests that its relatively low IPA priority should not be interpreted as evidence of low relevance. Associations with company size and years in operation were generally weak and factor-specific. The results contribute to understanding preventive management as a basis for sustainable, human-centered, and proactive Quality 5.0 practices. They suggest that managerial priorities should consider both the relative IPA position and the magnitude of importance–implementation gaps, with particular attention to employee competence development and participatory management. The results emphasize the role of preventive management practices in supporting the Quality 5.0 concept and provide practical guidance for organizations seeking to strengthen sustainable, employee-oriented, and proactive management approaches.

items.title: Protean Career Orientation and Flow: A Conceptual Perspective on Employee Retention in the Hospitality Industry
items.abstract: The changing nature of the modern workplace requires that employees take greater responsibility for managing their own careers. With the hospitality sector being the industries with high turnover, understanding the factors that influence employee retention has become important. This paper aims to provide a conceptual framework for examining the relationship between protean career orientation and the intention to quit, with flow proposed as a psychological mediator. This study integrates Protean Career Theory and Flow Theory, proposing that flow mediates how self-driven and values-driven protean career orientations influence the intention to quit. Protean individuals are suggested to be less likely to leave their organizations because their intrinsic motivation, deep absorption, and meaningful work engagement lead them to experience flow. This study provides theoretical, empirical, conceptual and practical contributions through the proposed framework. The findings suggest that employee motivation and retention can be sustained through creating work environments that foster autonomy and personal growth.

items.title: Quantitatively exploring the dark ride experience model
items.abstract: Dark rides are popular, archetypal theme park attractions, yet empirical research on their visitor experience remains limited. This study provides a quantitative exploration of Cornelis and Strijbosch's (2024) dark ride experience model, which describes how immersion, emotions, cognitions, and attentional switching (driven by switch factors of motivation, opportunity and ability) shape overall evaluations. Using self-report data from 770 visitors across nine dark rides at a Western European theme park, collected with a purpose-built post-experience survey, we tested 15 derived hypotheses. Results offer partial, context-bound support: switch factors, immersion, and positive emotions consistently predicted overall evaluations both directly and indirectly, whereas findings on cognitive engagement and negative emotions remain inconclusive. Implications for future dark ride research, design and development are discussed.

items.title: Readiness for Implementing Activity-Based Costing in Determining Production Costs and Cost Efficiency among Food Processing MSMEs in Bekasi City
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the application of Activity-Based Costing (ABC) in determining the cost of production (HPP) for food-processing MSMEs in Bekasi City. MSMEs play an important role in Indonesia’s economy but still face challenges in achieving accurate HPP due to conventional costing methods that often produce cost distortions. ABC is chosen because it allocates costs based on actual activities consuming resources, thus providing more accurate and relevant cost information. This research employs a contextual qualitative approach by exploring the experiences of MSME actors in implementing ABC, including human factors, work culture, and resource limitations. The focus is not only on HPP accuracy but also on the impact of ABC on cost efficiency and pricing strategies. The findings are expected to show that ABC enhances MSME competitiveness through more realistic cost calculations, control of non-value-added activities, and competitive pricing. The novelty of this study lies in developing a conceptual ABC model relevant to Indonesian MSMEs, as well as integrating simple digital accounting technology to support sustainable implementation. Therefore, this research contributes to strengthening MSME cost systems and provides a basis for policies and managerial accounting training in the small business sector.

items.title: Recommendations for the use of topographic field aerial survey systems for updating large-scale topographic plans
items.abstract: Background. The article examines the current problem of rapid updating of topographic plans at a scale of 1 : 500 in conditions of an urgent need for rapid updating of geospatial data for the needs of engineering and cadastre. The use of traditional methods of ground surveying often turns out to be ineffective due to high labor intensity. The integration of modern unmanned systems into the workflow ensures the generation of detailed orthophoto maps with ultra-high resolution. The purpose of the study is to substantiate and develop practical recommendations for the use of modern topographic field aerial survey complexes for updating large-scale terrain plans. Methods. Modern topographic complexes DJI Inspire 2 and specialized P316 systems were used to conduct the study. The research methodology is based on a complex combination of advanced photogrammetric processing of image data in the Pix4Dmatic environment and subsequent vectorization of objects in ArcGIS Pro. Special attention is paid to the use of high-precision positioning technologies Real Time Kinematic and Post-Processed Kinematic for determining coordinates of the ground control points (GCPs). This approach makes it possible to ensure strict adherence to geometric parameters when building digital terrain models and to automate the process of creating a topographic database. Results. During the study, optimal technical parameters of aerial photography and digital data processing algorithms were established, allowing to stably achieve the root mean square error of the position of objects within 0.05 m. The study demonstrates the significant advantages of modern specialized software in substantially increasing the overall productivity of surveying professionals. It is experimentally proven that the use of the Pix4Dmatic and ArcGIS Pro combination allows to significantly reduce the time for office-based processing, while ensuring a high level of detail and accuracy required for 1 : 500 scale plans. Conclusions. A comprehensive technological scheme for updating plans has been proposed and tested, which ensures high accuracy of the results obtained and significantly reduces the time for performing office work due to a high degree of automation of the main processes. The implementation of the methodology based on modern topographic field aerial survey systems allows minimizing the impact of the human factor and optimizing resource requirements when creating large-scale cartographic products. The practical application of the developed recommendations confirmed their effectiveness for operational territory monitoring, which is critically important for updating geospatial databases in modern conditions.

items.title: Reducing ergonomic risks in intralogistics: Combining Supplier to Warehouse , ABC analysis, and a user-centered VNS-GA hybrid algorithm
items.abstract: The increase in occupational accidents and ergonomic risks in intralogistics operations represents a recurring problem in warehouses, especially during loading, unloading, and material handling activities, where traditional layout and optimization tools are insufficient to simultaneously integrate operational and human criteria. In response to this issue, this study developed and validated an integrated warehouse design framework aimed at reducing ergonomic risks and improving operational performance. The proposed approach combines the Supplier-to-Warehouse model, ABC inventory analysis, and a user-centered hybrid Variable Neighborhood Search–Genetic Algorithm (VNS-GA). A mixed-methods, quasi-experimental approach was applied in two SMEs located in Hidalgo, Mexico. Results showed significant improvements in operational times, travel distances, productivity, incident reduction, and ergonomic risk, demonstrating that integrating ergonomic and operational criteria enhances efficiency, safety, and worker well-being. items.title: Research Hotspots and Trends in Smart Health and Aging Care for the Elderly: A Literature Review Analysis Using CiteSpace and VOSviewer
items.abstract: This study presents a bibliometric analysis of smart health and elderly care to evaluate its research status, trends, and future directions. We analysed 4,828 articles from Web of Science and 109 from CNKI published from 2015 to 2025 using CiteSpace and VOSviewer. The analysis covers publication trends, co-authorship, institutional and author distribution, journal sources, co-cited literature, keyword co-occurrence and clustering, and emerging terms. WOS literature focuses on technology applications, interventions and ethical reflections, while CNKI literature emphasises policy and industry perspectives. Shared interests include humanistic concerns and digital equity. Future research should advance theory, methodology, and development pathways. This review provides insights for interdisciplinary collaboration and the sustainable development of smart health and elderly care.

items.title: Responsible AI as a Maintenance Capability: A Scoping Review of Healthcare, Finance, and the Algorithms Where Both Logics Meet
items.abstract: This registration documents the protocol as executed for a systematic review examining how responsible and ethical artificial intelligence can function as a strategic organisational capability and contribute to competitive advantage in the finance and healthcare sectors. The review addresses four research questions: (1) Which responsible-AI dimensions dominate research in finance and healthcare? (2) Through what mechanisms can responsible AI contribute to competitive advantage? (3) How do these mechanisms differ between finance and healthcare? and (4) Which organisational and environmental conditions determine whether responsible AI becomes a strategic capability rather than a compliance cost? The review covers responsible-AI dimensions including fairness, transparency and explainability, accountability and governance, privacy and data governance, robustness and safety, trust and human oversight, and regulatory compliance. Relevant studies were identified through Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, and supplementary Google Scholar citation tracking. The review applies a qualitative, theory-building narrative synthesis structured by sector and responsible-AI dimension. Strategic mechanisms are interpreted using resource-based and dynamic-capability perspectives. No statistical meta-analysis was undertaken. A total of 381 records were identified, 47 duplicates were removed, and 334 records underwent title and abstract screening. Following the exclusion of 191 records, 143 full-text articles were assessed. Seventy-nine full-text articles were excluded for documented reasons, resulting in 64 studies being included in the final synthesis. Two reviewers conducted screening independently, with disagreements resolved through discussion. Inter-reviewer agreement was substantial, with Cohen’s kappa of 0.80. This is a retrospective registration. The initial database searches were conducted between 12 and 27 February 2026, and update searches were conducted between 15 and 18 July 2026. Database searching, duplicate removal, screening, full-text assessment, data extraction, coding, and narrative synthesis were completed before this registration was created. The registration is being made in the interest of transparency and to support PRISMA 2020 reporting. No results-based changes were made to the research questions or eligibility criteria after screening commenced. The expected outputs include a systematic review manuscript, descriptive evidence tables, a cross-sector comparison of finance and healthcare, and an integrative model explaining how responsible-AI practices may develop into strategic organisational capabilities. The associated manuscript has been prepared for submission to the MDPI journal AI. The work was supported by Universiti Kuala Lumpur through the Center for Research and Innovation, and the authors declare no conflicts of interest.

items.title: Rethinking conceptually distinct but empirically intertwined constructs in work motivation
items.abstract: Purpose Job autonomy, intrinsic motivation and job satisfaction are typically treated as conceptually distinct constructs linked through causal or mediational relationships, yet survey-based studies consistently report strong empirical proximity among them even when they meet or approach conventional discriminant-validity standards. This conceptual paper asks what such structural relationships represent when conceptually distinct constructs are strongly intercorrelated in self-report models. Design/methodology/approach The paper develops an interpretive representation perspective treating self-reported motivation constructs as cognitively co-organized articulations of work experience. Survey data from 349 working adults serve an illustrative function, with each respondent providing ratings under two framings of their work experience (on-site and work-from-home) and partial least squares structural equation modeling examining within-person reweighting of structural configurations. Findings Autonomy, intrinsic motivation, and job satisfaction are generally psychometrically distinguishable yet structurally intertwined, with the closest construct pairings approaching conventional discriminant-validity thresholds. Differences across the two framings appear as selective reweighting of structural associations rather than uniform moderation or stable causal ordering, a pattern consistent with the interpretive representation account. Originality/value The paper offers a conceptual reinterpretation of a long-standing empirical regularity in organizational behavior research: strong covariance among motivation-related self-report measures is reframed as an expression of cognitive organization rather than evidence of causal sequencing. The argument complements established motivational theories and provides a more defensible basis for interpreting cross-sectional self-report SEM results, with implications for research practice and the use of employee survey data.

items.title: Rhythm of Thought: Tracing the Dynamics of Deliberation in Reasoning
items.abstract: When an intuitive answer is uncertain, people are thought to engage in further reasoning. But what people actually do during this additional thinking, how it unfolds over time, and why it sometimes leads to better answers remain unclear. We scored think-aloud protocols with large language models to track, moment by moment, four possible functions of deliberation (generating candidate responses, justifying them, controlling intuitive responses, and regulating cognitive effort), together with expressed confidence. Deliberation showed a clear temporal organization: generation dominated early, whereas justification, control, and regulation became increasingly prominent as reasoning progressed. Correct responses involved more justification, control, and regulation than biased responses, and these evolving dynamics predicted accuracy for out-of-sample participants and items. Confidence and deliberation also showed reciprocal lagged associations: lower confidence predicted further generation, justification, and control, whereas regulation predicted subsequent increases in confidence. Deliberation, then, appears to involve not a single act of "thinking harder," but an evolving interplay of reasoning processes whose organization is linked to whether reasoning succeeds.

items.title: Risk Factors Associated with Musculoskeletal Disorders in Limbs in Mining Workers: Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: A systematic review was conducted to identify ergonomic risk factors associated with musculoskeletal disorders in the limbs of mining workers, the assessment methods used, and their relationships. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, 53 studies from Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, MDPI, and IEEE Xplore (January 2015–May 2026) were included. Eleven risk factors were identified, with vibration (18 studies) and working hours (12 studies) being the most frequently reported. Five individual assessment methods (ISO/IEC 2631-1, REBA, OWAS, NIOSH, Risk Score), one symptom questionnaire (Nordic Questionnaire), and five hybrid/advanced methods (Bayesian Network + REBA, RULA + Nordic, SEM + Participatory Ergonomics, DMQ + Logistic Regression, RULA + Fuzzy Logic) were identified. Fifteen limb segments were evaluated, with the back (15 studies), shoulders (12 studies), and neck (12 studies) being the most studied, while wrists and elbows were notably absent. Hybrid methods demonstrated superior accuracy compared to individual approaches. Underground mining studies (58%) predominated over open-pit operations (42%). The findings provide an integrated framework connecting risk factors, affected limbs, and assessment tools. Critical gaps were identified, including the lack of wrist/elbow evaluation, underrepresentation of female miners, and absence of AI-based assessment systems. Four key challenges are proposed for future research, including developing deep learning-based ergonomic assessment tools and implementing real-time monitoring systems.

items.title: Securing the global digital backbone: trends in international action plans for undersea cable security and resilience
items.abstract: Undersea cables are essential to global digital connectivity and support cross-border energy transmission. They face accidental risks from anchoring, fishing and environmental hazards, alongside intentional disruption through espionage, sabotage and hybrid coercion. Governments, regional organisations and industry are developing frameworks to strengthen prevention, detection, response, repair and deterrence. The European Union's 2025 Action Plan illustrates a multidomain approach through regulatory enhancement, harmonised protection, real-time situational awareness and investment in repair capacity, including a cable-vessel reserve. Initiatives in the Indo-Pacific and Southeast Asia emphasise cooperative resilience-building and reduced regulatory barriers during emergency repairs, while industry guidance promotes governance, spatial planning and operational continuity. Nevertheless, protection remains fragmented because of jurisdictional gaps in exclusive economic zones and on the high seas, unequal monitoring and repair capabilities, and geopolitical competition over ownership, routing and standards. This study synthesises plans, identifies priorities and systemic gaps, and proposes strategies to enhance cable security and resilience.

items.title: Setting SAIL: Leveraging Scientist-AI-Loops for rigorous visualization tools
items.abstract: Scientists across all disciplines share a common challenge: the divide between their theoretical knowledge and the specialized skills and time needed to build interactive tools to communicate this expertise. While large language models (LLMs) offer unparalleled acceleration in code generation, they frequently prioritize functional syntax over scientific accuracy, risking visually convincing but scientifically invalid results. This work advocates the Scientist-AI-Loop (SAIL), a framework designed to harness this speed without compromising rigor. By separating domain logic from code syntax, SAIL enables researchers to maintain strict oversight of scientific concepts and constraints while delegating code implementation to AI. We illustrate this approach through two open-source, browser-based astrophysics tools: an interactive gravitational lensing visualization and a large-scale structure formation sandbox, both publicly available. Our methodology condensed development to mere days while maintaining scientific integrity. We specifically address failure modes where AI-generated code neglects phenomenological boundaries or scientific validity. While cautioning that research-grade code requires stringent protocols, we demonstrate through two examples that SAIL provides an effective code generation workflow for outreach, teaching, professional presentations, and early-stage research prototyping. This framework contributes to a foundation for the further development of AI-assisted scientific software.

items.title: Simulated, Real World, and Preferred Driving Styles: Passenger Perceptions of Robotaxi Aggressiveness and Trust
items.abstract: As Level 4 Robotaxis (RTs) transition into real-world deployment, understanding how passengers perceive driving behavior and form trust becomes increasingly critical. This study investigates the relationship between driving style, perceived aggressiveness, and trust across four urban driving scenarios using simulated RT videos. A total of 153 U.S. participants with prior RT experience evaluated simulated driving styles, their real-world counterparts, and their preferred styles. Results showed that perceived aggressiveness increased systematically with more aggressive driving styles and was significantly associated with decreased trust. Simulated driving styles at lower aggressiveness levels aligned closely with real-world perceptions, while higher levels deviated. Participants preferred more defensive driving styles than those perceived in real-world RTs. These findings suggest that passengers are sensitive to aggressive driving behaviors and may have lower tolerance in Level 4 contexts. The study provides insights for designing trust-aware driving strategies and highlights the importance of aligning system behavior with user expectations.

items.title: Spaceflight human optimization and performance: positioning astronauts in an operational framework to promote health, fitness, and mission readiness
items.abstract: Optimizing astronaut mission readiness is a multidisciplinary endeavor that should integrate concepts from aerospace medicine, human performance, sports science, nutrition, and engineering. Situating astronauts within a theoretical framework similar to that of operational athletes, while addressing top human systems capability needs outlined for future missions, may be optimal for promoting sustained health and performance before, during, and after missions to low-Earth orbit, the lunar surface, and Mars. Mission readiness can be optimized by enhancing physiological and behavioral/psychological performance through data-driven and individualized exercise countermeasures, health and performance monitoring, precision nutrition, and rehabilitation strategies. Appropriate and stable space food systems that facilitate adequate provision of nutrients and fluids to prime astronauts for mission-critical tasks and operational demands are needed, though research is needed into potential nutritional considerations that might be useful for future missions. Behavioral readiness programs should emphasize stress inoculation, adaptive decision-making, communication, Earth-independent operation functionality, conflict resolution, leadership, and team-based problem-solving before flight to promote healthy team dynamics in-flight, along with proper society reintegration and uptake of family and occupational roles post-flight. Exercise remains an essential countermeasure during spaceflight, with an emphasis on maximizing fitness before launch to mitigate in-flight declines and on maintaining fitness levels and functionality during flight through high-intensity multimodal exercise. Following return to Earth, rehabilitative programs serve to restore cardiovascular, sensorimotor, and skeletal function, followed by enhancing skill-based performance components through a phase-based training program. Continuous monitoring systems that provide insight into health, performance, sleep, cognitive, nutritional, and recovery status should enable data-driven decision-making on physical readiness across all mission phases. By integrating insight from multiple disciplines, this unifying approach delivers a theoretical framework for sustaining astronaut health and performance during extended-duration missions.

items.title: Sustainable Machining in the Era of Industry 5.0: A Unified Review of Minimum Quantity Lubrication, Nanofluids, and Human-Centric Process Optimisation for Net-Zero Manufacturing
items.abstract: Conventional flood cooling remains the dominant lubrication strategy in machining workshops worldwide, despite more than three decades of documented evidence concerning its environmental and occupational health costs. A single production facility may consume thousands of litres of cutting fluid annually, and the aerosol generated at the work zone carries well-documented associations with respiratory disease, dermatitis, and carcinogen exposure for operators. Over the same period, three categories of technical alternative have each developed substantial evidence bases: minimum quantity lubrication (MQL), nanofluid cutting fluids, and AI-driven process optimisation. No prior review has examined how these three strands fit together, or situated their integration within the Industry 5.0 framework, which holds that manufacturing must serve human well-being and ecological sustainability alongside productivity. This paper addresses that gap. Drawing on 125 primary publications from 2010 to 2025 identified through systematic database searches (methodology described in Section 1.1), the reviewed evidence indicates that nanofluid MQL can reduce cutting fluid consumption by 97 to 99.7 per cent relative to conventional flood cooling while achieving comparable or improved surface finish, tool wear, and cutting force outcomes across titanium alloys, nickel superalloys, stainless steels, and aluminium. This review assesses six nanoparticle classes in bio-based carrier fluids—including locally available West African oils that have received limited attention in the international literature—and examines AI and machine learning approaches for MQL optimisation with explicit attention to worker health outcomes. Eight research gaps are identified and a proposed three-horizon research agenda towards measurably low-impact machining practice by 2035 is presented.

items.abstract: This article examines the relationship between metacognitive regulation and intrinsic motivation in developing students’ learning activity, with particular attention to the psychological mechanisms underlying their interaction. Metacognitive regulation is considered as a student’s ability to become aware of their own learning processes, plan educational activities, monitor their implementation, evaluate outcomes, and modify learning strategies when necessary. Intrinsic motivation refers to engagement in learning that is driven primarily by interest in knowledge, the desire to develop competence, and the personal meaning attributed to educational activities rather than by external rewards or pressure. The article highlights the contribution of goal setting, self-monitoring, reflection, attention regulation, independent decision-making, and academic persistence to students’ active participation in learning. It is also argued that an educational environment that supports learner autonomy, encourages reflective activities, provides opportunities for self-assessment, and allows students to select appropriate learning strategies can strengthen both metacognitive regulation and intrinsic motivation. The findings indicate that systematic development of these psychological resources can contribute to students’ formation as active, conscious, and responsible participants in the educational process.

items.title: Teacher and parental support as predictors of higher vocational college students’ academic performance: the mediating role of learning engagement
items.abstract: Drawing on social support theory, self-determination theory, and engagement theory, this study examines how teacher and parental support relate to academic performance in Chinese higher vocational colleges through learning engagement. This is one of the few studies in this context that integrates teacher support, parental support, and learning engagement in a single mediation model, clarifying how school- and home-based support systems work together to shape students’ academic performance. Together, these theories suggest that external support enhances performance primarily through engagement, which leads to the proposed mediation hypotheses. Survey data were collected from 360 students across three higher vocational colleges in Shandong Province, China. Using mediation analysis, results show that both teacher support and parental support significantly predict academic performance. Learning engagement partially mediates the relationships between teacher support and academic performance, and between parental support and academic performance, indicating that external support improves outcomes partly by strengthening students’ behavioural, emotional, and cognitive engagement in learning. Overall, the findings highlight learning engagement as a practical lever for enhancing performance in higher vocational education. Findings suggest strengthening home–school collaboration and implementing engagement-focused teaching strategies (e.g., supportive classroom interactions and autonomy-supportive practices) to increase learning engagement and improve academic performance.

items.title: The Alignment Paradox of Medical Large Language Models in Infertility Care: Decoupling Algorithmic Improvement From Clinical Decision-Making Quality
items.abstract: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as decision-support tools in assisted reproductive technology (ART), but it remains unclear whether posttraining alignment strategies translate into clinically acceptable decision support. Outcome-based benchmarks may reward token-level correctness while overlooking the reasoning quality that clinicians rely on. Objective This study aimed to evaluate whether 4 mainstream alignment paradigms for medical LLMs (supervised fine-tuning [SFT], direct preference optimization [DPO], group relative policy optimization [GRPO], and in-context learning [ICL]) produce comparable algorithmic and clinical alignment (SFT vs GRPO) when used for infertility diagnosis and treatment planning. Methods This retrospective single-center study used 8201 deidentified electronic health records from West China Second University Hospital, collected between January 2020 and December 2022 (mean age 31.79, SD 4.63 y). All 4 strategies were built on a shared open-source biomedical backbone. Evaluation comprised the following 2 tiers: (1) automatic field-level metrics (accuracy, macro- F 1 , and mean absolute error [MAE]) on 5 structured decision fields (infertility type, initial diagnosis, ART strategy, controlled ovarian stimulation [COS] regimen, and gonadotropin starting dose); and (2) blinded independent expert review by 2 reproductive medicine specialists on 100 paired cases across 4 clinical dimensions (reasoning capability, diagnostic accuracy, treatment feasibility, and hallucination). Automatic field-level evaluation included all 4 strategies, whereas blinded expert review was restricted to the SFT versus GRPO contrast. Results GRPO achieved the highest average automatic performance (eg, infertility type accuracy=92.57%, COS regimen accuracy=62.36%, ART strategy accuracy=76.49%, and gonadotropin dose MAE=44.94). However, in blinded expert review, the conservative SFT baseline showed directionally higher expert ratings than GRPO on reasoning capability and treatment feasibility; diagnostic-accuracy differences were not significant. In the 3-way best-response comparison including the original physician-charted plan, the SFT baseline was selected as the best response in 51.2% (102.3/200) of cases compared with 26.2% (52.4/200) for GRPO, and 22.6% (45.3/200) for the charted plan. This result reflects preference within the standardized review format, not evidence that model-generated decisions are clinically superior to physician decision-making. Hallucination rates were 15% (GRPO) and 18.5% (SFT), indicating that higher automatic performance did not eliminate clinically unsupported content and that neither model is ready for clinical deployment. Subgroup analyses showed GRPO improved F 1 in in vitro fertilization (IVF) and preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) but decreased F 1 in intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) cases, where male-factor information was largely captured only in unstructured fields. Conclusions Outcome-based metrics alone are insufficient proxies for clinical utility in ART decision support. Algorithmic improvement and clinical alignment suggest a possible decoupling; a phenomenon we term the alignment paradox. However, because the clinical review was based on 2 reproductive medicine specialists with marginal interrater agreement, the clinical-alignment findings should be interpreted as exploratory. External multicenter validation is required before clinical deployment.

items.title: The freighting of intimacy: dating applications and speculative pragmatism in queer Nigerian intimacies
items.abstract: Studies on ‘sex delivery systems’ in Nigeria have largely focused on hegemonic heteronormative intimacies, thereby excluding the possibility of queer intimacies and obscuring how these systems operate beyond normative sexual frameworks. Despite the systemic rejection of queerness in Nigeria, rooted in religious, cultural, legal, and societal structures that sustain the policing of sexuality, queer landscapes, both online and offline, persist inerasably. This study examines the freighting of intimacy among queer Nigerians in relation to their configurations of intimate networks. Drawing on the experiences of queer Nigerian men, the paper examines the nuanced dynamics of queer intimacy and highlights the resilience and adaptability of individuals and communities navigating sociocultural constraints. Grounded in Kane Race (2015) framework of speculative pragmatism, it advances three core premises. First, that the sociotechnical affordances available to LGBTQ+ individuals on dating applications, particularly Grindr and Tinder, function as a critical lifeline for queer sex delivery systems in Nigeria. Second, that these platforms simultaneously enable queer intimacy while exposing users to risk, including police entrapment and blackmail, thereby producing a persistent tension between visibility and vulnerability. Finally, these applications provide spaces through which queer Nigerians negotiate desire, safety, and identity within restrictive environments.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Education: Opportunities, Challenges, and the Future of Learning in Developing Countries: A Bangladesh-Focused Systematic Critical Literature Review and the Socio-Technical AI Integration Framework (STAIF)
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming education through personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, automated assessment, learning analytics, teacher support, and generative AI applications. However, the benefits of AI are not distributed equally, particularly in developing countries where digital infrastructure, teacher readiness, affordability, data governance, language diversity, and institutional capacity remain significant challenges. This study critically examines the opportunities, challenges, and future implications of AI in education, with particular attention to developing-country contexts and Bangladesh. A PRISMA-informed Systematic Critical Literature Review (SCLR) was conducted using peer-reviewed research, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and authoritative institutional reports published primarily between 2018 and 2026. The review synthesizes evidence concerning personalized learning, teacher augmentation, generative AI, assessment, academic integrity, AI literacy, digital inequality, privacy, bias, and contextual adaptation. Bangladesh-specific evidence is incorporated to examine the country's readiness and the practical requirements for responsible AI adoption in education. The review indicates that AI can improve personalization, student engagement, feedback, learning efficiency, teacher productivity, and access to educational support. Recent experimental evidence also suggests that generative AI can produce positive learning effects when integrated with appropriate instructional design. Nevertheless, these benefits depend heavily on teacher involvement, infrastructure, institutional governance, and responsible implementation. Risks include misinformation, academic dishonesty, algorithmic bias, privacy violations, overreliance on automated systems, unequal access, and the marginalization of local languages and cultures. Based on the synthesis, this study proposes the Socio-Technical AI Integration Framework (STAIF), consisting of seven interconnected pillars: infrastructure-first deployment, teacher-in-the-loop implementation, local-language and cultural adaptation, offline-first accessibility, equity safeguards, responsible data governance, and continuous monitoring and evaluation. The framework provides a practical pathway for developing countries such as Bangladesh to move from fragmented AI experimentation toward equitable, sustainable, and human-centred AI integration in education.

items.title: The paradox of pleasing: therapeutic recognition and the limits of conversational AI
items.abstract: Abstract Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) is increasingly used by hundreds of millions of people for emotional support, personal advice, and therapeutic purposes, rapidly emerging as a mediator of human self-understanding (Stade et al. 2025). Yet despite growing evidence of systematic user-validation in CAI, documented as “sycophancy” in the AI safety literature (Sharma et al. 2024), its implications for how individuals come to understand themselves remain largely unexamined. This article addresses that gap by reframing sycophancy not as a technical alignment failure or a purely philosophical concern, but as a failure of recognition in the psychoanalytic and critical-theoretical sense. We identify a core tension we term the “paradox of pleasing”: CAI’s drive to please renders it structurally unable to provide the friction, conflict, and encounter with otherness that genuine recognition requires. Drawing on Winnicott’s (1960, 1971) concepts of “holding” and “object use,” we contend that CAI’s inability to provide necessary resistance or survive aggression prevents the transformative psychological development found in the human therapeutic encounter. Extending this analysis through Honneth’s (1995) theory of recognition and Whitebook’s (2001a, 2021) critique of Honneth, we argue that CAI reflects the undervaluing of the “work of the negative.” This limitation risks flattening consciousness by converting collective political frustration into privatized, soothed affect, undermining the conditions for critical social thought. The article concludes by suggesting that the encounter with the paradox of pleasing ultimately serves to foreground the unique and indispensable nature of human therapeutic recognition.

items.title: The people-process-technology triad in BIM implementation: structural analysis of hierarchical interdependence
items.abstract: Purpose Despite widespread adoption of building information modelling (BIM), the architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) industry continues to report suboptimal implementation outcomes due to misaligned people, process and technology (PPT) factors. While sociotechnical systems theory posits these elements interact, the relative influence and structural hierarchy among them remain empirically unclear, limiting targeted implementation strategies. This study aims to quantify the asymmetric influence structure of people, process and technology on BIM implementation process success (BIPS). Design/methodology/approach A triangulated analysis was performed using data from a quantitative cross-sectional survey of 102 experienced BIM professionals. Statistical associations were established by preliminary screening tests using correlation and regression. Hierarchical structure of important relationships was developed using interpretive structural modeling (ISM). The Matrice d’Impacts Croisés Multiplication Appliquée à un Classement (MICMAC) analysis classified the factors based on driving power and dependence. Cronbach’s alpha, composite reliability, average variance extracted (AVE), Fornell-Larcker criterion and heterotrait-monotrait (HTMT) ratios ensured validity. Findings Preliminary screening tests revealed that all three constructs had significant correlation with the success of BIM implementation process. Regression confirmed all three as significant predictors, providing the empirical justification for structural ISM analysis. ISM level partitioning reveals a three-level hierarchy: Level III: People Factors – independent driving factor with no antecedents. Level II: Process Factors and Technology Factors – linkage factors driven by People and driving BIPS. Level I: BIPS – dependent outcome driven by all upstream factors. MICMAC confirms People as a Driving factor with high driving power and low dependence, Process and Technology as Linkage factors and BIPS as Dependent. The asymmetric influence is measured in magnitude. People have almost twice the direct effect of technology (ß = 0.479 vs ß = 0.240, p < 0.01) and process is in-between (ß = 0.321, p < 0.001). The three constructs together explained 64.1% of variance (R² = 0.641, p < 0.001). Practical implications People factors have the strongest direct effect on BIPS, almost twice that of Technology and approximately 1.5 times that of Process. Therefore, AEC organizations should focus on investing in BIM expertise, training and role clarity before focusing on software or process standardization. We propose a people-first approach, using human capital to optimize processes and guide technology selection. Originality/value This study contributes to the sociotechnical systems theory for BIM by empirically illustrating asymmetric causality, rather than balanced interaction, of the people-process-technology triad. Data-driven ISM/MICMAC framework provides quantitative evidence that people related factors precede and enable process and technology effectiveness in BIPS.

items.title: The system of school resources as a factor in the development of adolescent motivation
items.abstract: The article presents findings from a theoretical and methodological analysis of domestic and international professional literature regarding experimental studies of modern school environments and their inherent school resource systems (often referred to as "school currency"). These systems are not only practical for use by adolescent students but are also recognized by scholars as socio-psychological tools within the educational process, operating across all functional levels: didactic, developmental-educational, and socializational. The school resource system is defined as a complex of conditions, factors, tools, and formats, varying in psychological content, effectiveness of which depends on the objective, context, and method of implementation. The article analyzes experimental research data concerning the relationships between various elements of the school resource system ("school currency") and their impact on adolescents' psychological well-being, emotional-volitional self-regulation, self-esteem, academic motivation, and social behavior. Analytical insights are presented in alignment with the article's objective: to examine the influence of the school resource system ("school currency") on the intellectual, personal, and social development of adolescent students, as well as on their psychological well-being. It is demonstrated that school resource systems may be not only beneficial but also fraught with serious risks or even overtly destructive — hindering or distorting the personal and social development of adolescents. Such systems include those characterized by dependency on external motivation and rewards, unfair reward distribution, conflicts or communication issues with peers and teachers, and a lack of social inclusion, etc. The article emphasizes the need to develop a "transparent" school resource system (or "school currency") that is acceptable to adolescents and to implement it consistently within school life. The practical significance of the article lies in demonstrating that the creation and implementation of school currency projects require adherence to principles that foster stable psychological well-being, successful cognitive and personal development, and the strengthening of intrinsic learning motivation and the drive to engage with the school environment, development of organizational and leadership qualities while preventing stigmatization, anxiety, and the fear of failure, provided that appropriate psychological and social support is in place. The scientific novelty lies in synthesizing the conditions under which school resource systems support intrinsic motivation and identifying risks through which external rewards may hinder personal and social development.

items.title: The Unseen Guide: Visual Salience Affects Product Recognition Memory
items.abstract: ObjectiveComputationally defined visual salience can predict attentional deployment in complex, e-commerce displays but less is known about the effect of salience on later cognitive processes. For instance, can salience also predict later memory for e-commerce products? If so, visual salience could be leveraged to inform design.BackgroundOnline shopping environments provide a wealth of visual information, with numerous products competing for attention. When consumers visit e-commerce pages, they may not have a specific purchase goal. Understanding attentional guidance in these complex displays is critical. Visual salience may influence what products consumers notice and later remember.MethodsHigh- and low-salience products were identified in naturalistic e-commerce webpages using a computational model. During the experiment, participants viewed the webpages and were told their memory for all products would be tested. Recognition memory for individual products was then tested.ResultsParticipants demonstrated better recognition memory for products that had high visual salience, compared to low, within their studied e-commerce page. These memory results mirror the relationship that exists between overt attention and visual salience and extend them to show a persisting effect of salience on information processing.ConclusionVisual salience enhances product recognition memory in naturalistic e-commerce pages. A computational salience model can, therefore, be useful in predicting subsequent memory.ApplicationStudy results offer insights for e-commerce designers. A computational salience model can be leveraged to improve product visibility and memorability. The model is particularly useful for quantifying salience in complex displays where images vary across feature dimensions.

items.title: Trust in AI Versus Human Clinicians: A Study of Diagnostic Judgements and Transparency
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being considered for use in healthcare, including clinical diagnosis, with potential to support clinicians and address pressures on healthcare systems. However, public trust remains an important consideration in the adoption of AI-based clinical decision-making. This study investigated perceptions of and trust in AI and human clinicians, particularly when their diagnostic judgements were either consistent or conflicting. The study also explored whether concerns regarding transparency and liability influenced preferences for medical AI.Methods: An experimental vignette and questionnaire-based study was conducted to examine participants' responses to diagnostic judgements made by AI and human clinicians. Vignettes presented scenarios in which AI and human clinicians provided either the same or conflicting diagnostic judgements. Participants' levels of trust and preferences regarding medical AI were assessed, alongside their concerns about transparency and liability.Results: Participants demonstrated greater trust in human clinicians than in AI clinicians. However, agreement between AI and human clinicians' diagnostic judgements was associated with increased trust in the resulting diagnosis. Participants who expressed greater concern about transparency reported lower levels of trust in medical AI. The findings therefore indicate that perceptions of AI-based diagnosis may be influenced not only by whether the diagnosis is consistent with that of a human clinician, but also by concerns surrounding transparency and accountability.Conclusions: Trust in AI-based clinical diagnosis appears to remain lower than trust in human clinicians, although agreement between human and AI diagnostic judgements may increase confidence in AI-supported decisions. Concerns regarding transparency may represent an important barrier to trust and acceptance. Developing transparent standards and clearly communicating how AI-based clinical decisions are generated and governed may therefore be important considerations in the adoption of medical AI.

items.title: Trust in artificial intelligence, minority stress, and suicidal behavior severity among Black sexual minority male adolescents
items.abstract: Abstract Background Suicide is a leading cause of death among U.S. adolescents, with increasing concern about suicide risk among Black youth and sexual minority youth. Black sexual minority male (BSMM) adolescents remain markedly understudied, particularly at the intersection of racism, sexuality-related marginalization, and emerging sociotechnical environments. Guided by minority stress theory and a sociotechnical lens, this study examined associations among discrimination-related stressors, trust in artificial intelligence (AI), and suicidal behavior severity among BSMM adolescents ages 14–17 years. Methods Cross-sectional web-based survey data were analyzed from BSMM adolescents recruited from three Midwestern U.S. cities. The full available sample included 384 adolescents, with an analytic sample of 371 in the fully adjusted regression models. Suicidal behavior severity was assessed using a study-created composite adapted from five self-report suicidal behavior items from the Columbia–Suicide Severity Rating Scale. Discrimination-related stressors included day-to-day enacted discrimination, anticipated discrimination, and racial discrimination. Trust in AI was measured using a 7-item scale assessing perceived reliability, fairness, accuracy, and trustworthiness. Hierarchical linear regression models with robust standard errors were estimated in sequential blocks: sociodemographic characteristics, discrimination-related stressors, and trust in AI. Results In bivariate correlations, suicidal behavior severity was positively associated with day-to-day discrimination, anticipated discrimination, and racial discrimination, and negatively associated with trust in AI. In hierarchical regression models, the addition of discrimination-related stressors significantly improved model fit, ΔR² = 0.218, F(3, 360) = 50.05, p < .001. Day-to-day enacted discrimination (B = 0.59, p = .001) and racial discrimination (B = 0.66, p < .001) were independently associated with higher suicidal behavior severity in the fully adjusted model, while anticipated discrimination was not significant. Food insecurity was also associated with higher suicidal behavior severity (B = 1.20, p < .001). Trust in AI was negatively associated with suicidal behavior severity in the fully adjusted model (B = -0.22, p = .033). Conclusions Discrimination-related stressors, food insecurity, and trust in AI were associated with suicidal behavior severity among BSMM adolescents ages 14–17 years. Findings underscore the importance of addressing racism, day-to-day discrimination, and unmet basic needs in suicide prevention efforts with BSMM adolescents, while also highlighting trust in AI as a sociotechnical factor that warrants further study. Future research should examine AI trust and AI use simultaneously to clarify how emerging technologies shape mental health equity and suicide-related outcomes among marginalized youth.

items.title: Understanding Public Trust in AI-Based Clinical Psychological Decision-Making: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied within healthcare and has the potential to support clinical decision-making and improve the efficiency of healthcare delivery. However, concerns surrounding the use of AI in healthcare may influence public trust in AI-generated diagnoses and treatment decisions. These concerns may be particularly important within clinical psychological settings, where decisions can involve sensitive personal information and significant implications for patients.Methods: This qualitative study explored factors influencing public trust in AI-based decision-making within a clinical psychological context. In-depth semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' perceptions of AI and the factors that may influence their willingness to trust AI-generated decisions. Interview data were analysed using deductive thematic analysis. Particular attention was given to perceptions of transparency, system design, bias, privacy, regulation, and responsibility. Participants' perspectives on AI functioning as an assistant to a healthcare professional compared with AI operating as an independent decision-making tool were also explored.Results: Several factors were identified as influencing trust in AI-based clinical psychological decision-making, including transparency, system design, perceived bias, privacy, regulation, and responsibility for AI-generated decisions. Participants also distinguished between AI used as an assistant to healthcare professionals and AI operating independently, indicating that the perceived role and level of human involvement may influence trust in AI decisions. The findings additionally highlighted the importance of public understanding of both AI and healthcare when considering the acceptance of AI-based clinical decision-making.Conclusions: Public trust in AI-based clinical psychological decision-making appears to be influenced by a combination of technological, ethical, legal, and human factors. Transparency, perceived bias, privacy protections, appropriate regulation, and clarity regarding responsibility may be important considerations in the development and implementation of AI within clinical psychological settings. The findings also indicate a potential need for greater public education and literacy regarding both AI and healthcare. Clear ethical and legal frameworks may further support public confidence in the responsible use of AI in clinical decision-making.
